2	name: generate-project-instructions
3	description: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
4	---
5	
6	# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc
7	
8	This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
9	lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
10	projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
11	product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
12	different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
13	handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
14	re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
15	pack machinery run from the project's tree.
16	
17	The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:
18	
19	- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
20	  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
21	- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
22	  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
23	  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
24	  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
25	  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
26	  through the pack system rather than `@import`.
27	
28	The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
29	to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
30	reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
31	portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
32	up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.
33	
34	## 1. Gather the evidence
35	
36	Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
37	imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
38	PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
39	things, both grounded in what you actually find:
40	
41	- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
42	- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
43	  be sorted by owner (step 3).
44	
45	Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
46	question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.
47	
48	## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet
49	
50	A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:
51	
52	- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
53	  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
54	  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
55	- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
56	  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
57	  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
58	  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
59	- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
60	  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
61	  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
62	  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
63	- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
64	  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
65	  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
66	  isn't a facet worth a pack.
67	
68	**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
69	rules land in the project's own local pack.
70	
71	And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
72	or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
73	whatever the feature happens to be. A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or
74	that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable
75	spec and the suite that proves it. Encoding it as a pack check instead splits one feature's definition
76	across two systems and lands it in the one no test of the product ever reads. Pack-worthiness is a question
77	about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a requirements
78	gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.
79	
80	<example>
81	One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
82	`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
83	its local pack holds only what none of them own.
84	</example>
85	
86	Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
87	consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):
88	
89	- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
90	  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
91	  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
92	  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
93	  supports should say so or wait.
94	- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
95	- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
96	  placeholders helps nobody.
97	
98	Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
99	sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.
100	
101	## 3. Sort every candidate rule to the single facet that owns it
102	
103	For each rule from step 1, apply the **portability strip per facet**: delete from the rule everything
104	the facet doesn't keep, and see whether something meaningful survives.
105	
106	- Delete the product and the stack, keep the loop — survives? → the **class** pack (canon).
107	- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or
108	  **aspect**) pack (canon).
109	- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
110	- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.
111	
112	Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
113	any Node service" belongs to the canon `node` pack, not to this project's class pack, even if every
114	project of the class happens to use Node. Rewrite what lands in a canon pack project-agnostically and
115	parameterized, the way research-project does ("read *input* as whatever it means for your project").
116	
117	Then gate **every** pack-bound rule — canon or local — on the promotion ladder
118	([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)): a rule a deterministic **check** could enforce, or a
119	procedure with a nameable trigger a **skill** could carry, becomes that (in a canon seed it's flagged
120	as a check/skill candidate; in a local pack you author the check outright in the pack's `rules`, with
121	a red-first fixture) rather than settling as prose. What remains in a `RULES.md` is the always-relevant
122	judgment core of its facet — write more checks and less prose. Dedupe against the corpus: a rule the
123	basics baseline, an existing canon pack, or a skill already owns is not pack material at all.
124	
125	## 4. Write each pack
126	
127	Mint a pack for a facet only when its surviving rules clear the bar — several durable rules, not one
128	stray (a single rule joins the nearest existing pack, or waits as a handoff note). Each
129	`packs/<facet>/` needs four things (mirror `research-project/` and `chrome-extension/`):
130	
131	- **`RULES.md`** — the playbook, addressed to the *next* project sharing the facet, on day one. Open
132	  with the facet's one-line definition and "a default to adapt, not a contract". Principle-first, each
133	  rule carrying its why. It loads at session start for every declaring project, so every line pays
134	  rent — cover the facet, not everything you noticed.
135	- **`pack.mjs`** — the manifest. Class/domain/aspect packs: `always: false`, `marker: null`,
136	  `detect: null` (declaration is authoritative). Technology packs: add the `marker`/`detect`
137	  fingerprint when the repo carries a reliable one, so `--init` seeds the pack into a fresh
138	  declaration; the marker only *suspects* a pack is wanted, it never forces its declaration.
139	  Discovery is structural — the directory is the registration.
140	- **`README.md`** — the pack's rule table (section ≤5 words | how enforced), plus one provenance line
141	  naming the project it was distilled from.
142	- **Index entries** — a row in [packs/README.md](../../../../packs/README.md) and, for a new pack kind, the
143	  matching line in the corpus map ([README.md](../../../../README.md) — there is no agent-facing corpus index, #385).
144	
145	The acid test before proposing any pack: **a reader must not be able to tell which project it was
146	extracted from.** Any surviving repo path, command line, or product noun marks a rule that belonged in
147	the overlay.
148	
149	## 5. Write the project's own local pack(s)
150	
151	The project-specific residue lands in a **local pack** under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the
152	project's tree — the same pack machinery, run from the project instead of the canon. Most projects
153	need **one** general pack (name it for the project); segregate a **second** only when a distinct domain
154	earns its own bundle (the way the reference project split a general working pack from an
155	extractor-automation pack). Each local pack is a real pack:
156	
157	- **`pack.mjs`** — `{ id, detect: null, marker: null, prose: 'RULES.md', rules: [...], skills: [...] }`.
158	  A local pack is declared by hand, never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` stay null), as its
159	  namespaced token `local_packs/<name>` in `.claudinite-checks.json`; its id
160	  must be unique and may not shadow a canon pack.
161	- **`RULES.md`** — the always-loaded judgment core and the project's concrete values (real
162	  setup/run/verify commands, real paths, inputs, metrics, invariants). Keep it terse; anything a check
163	  or skill can carry doesn't belong here, and anything inferable from the code is omitted.
164	- **Checks** (`rules`) — the project-specific deterministic rules as `.mjs` modules listed on
165	  `pack.mjs`, each with a red-first fixture (`pack.test.mjs`) runnable by the project's own test suite.
166	  Local check modules stay dependency-free (they must load without the gitignored mount): return plain
167	  finding objects rather than importing the engine's helpers.
168	- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the project's activity-scoped procedures, bundled in the pack;
169	  a local pack may also *require* a canon skill by name.
170	- **Scheduled tasks** (`tasks/<name>/task.mjs` + its `task.md`) — first-class like every other slot:
171	  the repo's own scheduler discovers a local pack's tasks in the same scan that finds a canon pack's,
172	  gated by the project's declaration exactly the same way. So project-specific scheduled work belongs
173	  in a local task declaration (a self-contained module honoring the task contract, with its
174	  co-located worker doc), not an out-of-repo routine and not a cron of its own.
175	
176	The project's `CLAUDE.md` becomes a thin **routing map** to its local packs (and its genuine design
177	docs) — it does **not** `@import` the pack prose; the pack system injects the active local packs'
178	`RULES.md` at session start, the same as the canon packs'.
179	
180	## 6. Deliver through the owner's approval gates
181	
182	- **Every canon pack seed or refinement → a PR against Claudinite.** Minting or changing a *canon* pack
183	  is the owner's call, and the PR is that gate — no corpus change lands unattended
184	  ([the canon-curation README](../../../../.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/README.md)). From a consuming repo, never edit the read-only
185	  `.claudinite/` mount: open the Claudinite PR when the session can reach that repo; otherwise stage the
186	  seed as a **local pack** clearly marked as a proposed-canon facet and open a Claudinite issue pointing
187	  at it, so the promote stage lifts it centrally.
188	- **The project's local pack(s) → the project's normal branch/PR**, committed under
189	  `.claudinite/local_packs/` (tracked project content — the sync hook preserves it, the gitignore
190	  re-includes it). Declaring a **local** pack — as `local_packs/<name>` — is valid immediately (the
191	  engine discovers local packs from the repo), so the declaration lands in the same PR.
192	- **Declare a new *canon* pack** in `.claudinite-checks.json` only after it has merged and the mount
193	  re-synced — declaring a canon id the mounted registry doesn't know is an unknown-pack settings error;
194	  a *local* id is never that error. Note a pending canon declaration as a follow-up in the project PR.
195	- **Existing projects sharing a facet keep their local packs for now.** Once the canon pack lands, the
196	  growth dedup stage prunes what the canon newly owns; don't pre-trim against an unmerged pack.
197	
198	Close with a short report: each facet and its one-line definition, with its shelf verdict (declared /
199	refined / minted-to-canon / kept-local / left alone); the sort tally (rules sent to each canon pack /
200	the local pack / as a check vs. a skill vs. prose); and links to the PRs.

AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: >
  TLDR backend (app stack) — HTTP API v2 + Google JWT authorizer, one Lambda, DynamoDB single table.

Parameters:
  GoogleClientId:
    Type: String
    # Intentionally no default: an empty JWT-authorizer audience would accept ID tokens minted for
    # ANY Google app. This MUST be the Google Cloud OAuth "Web application" client id.
    Description: Google OAuth "Web application" client id — the JWT authorizer audience (also the extension's auth client_id).
    AllowedPattern: '.+'
    ConstraintDescription: GoogleClientId must be provided.
  AllowedExtensionOrigin:
    Type: String
    Default: '*'
    Description: >
      CORS allowed origin. Keep '*': API Gateway HTTP API v2 REJECTS the chrome-extension:// scheme in CORS
      AllowOrigins ("Invalid format for origin"), so the extension origin can't be set here. Not a security
      gap — writes are gated by the JWT authorizer and reads are public; the '*' is also what lets the
      extension reach the API under standard CORS (so it needs no host_permissions). The security boundary is
      the JWT authorizer, never browser CORS. (See dev/docs/architecture.md §6.3 / §12-A9 / §12-A10.)
  RateLimitPerMinute:
    Type: Number
    Default: 10
    Description: Max comments one author may post per minute (enforced by a TTL'd DynamoDB counter). 0 disables.
  MaxBodyBytes:
    Type: Number
    Default: 8192
  QueryLimit:
    Type: Number
    Default: 50
  EmailHashSalt:
    Type: String
    Default: ''
    NoEcho: true
    Description: >
      Server secret salting the stored one-way email hash (used for moderation only; the hash is never
      returned). Set to a long random string; rotating it disconnects old hashes from new ones.

Conditions:
  # Which environment this is, is derived from the STACK NAME — not an external parameter. Production
  # is the one canonical stack named `tldr-app`; its table name is then pinned (below) to the exact
  # legacy `tldr-comments`. Nothing passed at deploy time can make prod point at a different table.
  # Any other stack name (tldr-app-dev, or an ad-hoc tldr-app-<x>) is non-prod and gets its own
  # stack-scoped table, so dev/sandbox testing can never read or write prod data.
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref AWS::StackName, tldr-app]

Globals:
  Function:
    Runtime: nodejs22.x
    Architectures:
      - x86_64
    Timeout: 10
    MemorySize: 256
    Environment:
      Variables:
        NODE_OPTIONS: --enable-source-maps
        TABLE_NAME: !Ref CommentsTable
        MAX_BODY_BYTES: !Ref MaxBodyBytes
        QUERY_LIMIT: !Ref QueryLimit
        RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE: !Ref RateLimitPerMinute
        EMAIL_HASH_SALT: !Ref EmailHashSalt

Resources:
  CommentsTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    # The one irreplaceable-state resource. Retain on delete AND on replace; PITR for restore-to-second.
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      # prod (stack tldr-app) => the exact legacy name, HARD-CODED in source so it can't be overridden
      # from outside (renaming would REPLACE the table — see UpdateReplacePolicy and the frozen-KeySchema
      # note below). Any other stack => a stack-scoped table (e.g. tldr-app-dev => tldr-app-dev-comments),
      # so it's physically distinct from prod's data store.
      TableName: !If [IsProd, tldr-comments, !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-comments']
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST

stack_name = "tldr-app"
region = "il-central-1"
capabilities = "CAPABILITY_IAM"
resolve_s3 = true

# Executable requirements — the framework standard

The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests. The judgment layer — doc-first
red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is the
[spec-driven-product](../spec-driven-product/RULES.md) playbook; this pack is the mechanics that
implement it, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
kind).

## 1. The layout is the contract

- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
  not.
- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
  kind field. Cases are
  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
  must be red.

## 2. What the coverage gate checks

The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
edits the gate.

The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
entry as `config.spec`.

316 dev/docs/ui-testing-guideline.md
# UI testing with executable requirements — a portable guideline

A field guide for testing a UI the way this repo tests the extension's side panel and options page:
as **executable requirements**. It is **project-agnostic** — the principles hold for a Chrome
extension popup, a web app, a mobile screen, a CLI's rendered output. The point is the *practice of
UI testing*, not any one rendering technology; HTML rendering is one section near the end, not the
spine.

Two worked examples to read alongside it: this repo's
[`dev/requirements/`](../requirements/README.md), and the project it adapts,
[`missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator` `dev/requirements/`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/tree/main/dev/requirements).
The durable, cross-project testing lessons these build on live in the team corpus (`testingPractices.md`).

---

## 1. The problem this solves

Most UI test suites fail in one of a few predictable ways:

- **They rot.** A snapshot authored today goes red next week because the clock, locale, or timezone
  moved — not because the UI changed. People stop trusting it and regenerate baselines on autopilot.
- **They fake the very thing under test.** A test that stubs the exact boundary where the behavior
  lives (the tab actually opening, the element actually rendering) can only confirm the shape it
  asserts, never the runtime effect.
- **They drift from the product.** A hand-authored "expected" that mirrors what production *should*
  render is a parallel implementation; it diverges silently and can even encode a state the app never
  shows.
- **Nobody reads them for intent.** Unit tests assert mechanics; no one opens them to learn what the
  UI is *supposed* to do, so requirements live only in someone's head.
- **One mechanism is forced onto everything.** A pixel-snapshot gate is made to "cover" a click it
  can never observe, or a state its fixture can't reach — so the gate is green while the behavior is
  unverified.

Executable requirements attack all five at once.

## 2. The core idea

> A **numbered specification** of what the UI must do, where **every leaf requirement is claimed by
> exactly one executable case**, of exactly one **kind** of verification, whose **expected result is
> owned by a human** and whose **actual is produced by the real code**. Adding a requirement fails
> the build until a case proves it.

Five moving parts:

1. **A spec that is the source of truth** — numbered leaves, each a single testable statement.
2. **A bijection gate** — every leaf has exactly one case; every case names a real leaf. A new
   requirement with no case is red; a stray case is red.
3. **Kinds** — each leaf is verified by the *one mechanism it actually needs* (a render snapshot, a
   gesture/behavior test, a pure-logic assertion, an end-to-end run).
4. **Owner-owned expecteds** — the success criterion (a committed golden, a coded assertion) is
   approved by a human and never silently rewritten to go green.
5. **Real-code actuals** — the "actual" is produced by running the shipped UI code against faked
   *inputs*, never by a parallel re-implementation.

## 3. What to focus on (the principles)

These are the load-bearing ideas. Get these right and the file layout is a detail.

### 3.1 Doc-first, red by default
The spec drives the tests. Adding a leaf to the spec makes the build red until a case claims it — so

## 3. The kind vocabulary

Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:

- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
  — the bijection stays strict.
- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
  never in the default loop.

## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards

Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
states without losing the claim.

- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.

**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:

- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.

## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec

A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:

- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.

## 6. Rendering recipes per stack

- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
  package and unit tests share it.
- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
  the threshold.

## 7. The gallery is derived output

- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
  captioned storyboard strip.
- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.

## 8. Refresh is a review step

One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.

- **A UGC / moderation domain pack** (XSS-safe body, `RateLimitPerMinute`, `MaxBodyBytes`, `EmailHashSalt`, `denylist.mjs`, public reads) — real and load-bearing, but every rule I could ground states *what the product does*, and leaf `3.3` already claims the XSS one. Rejected under this repo's own standing rule, *A pack carries how we work — never what the product does* — the same mistake #121 made.
- **A "single-source vendoring / GENERATED files" pack** — fully homed by `basics` + `engineering-practices`; the `.gitattributes` `merge=ours` driver is literally a `basics` check.
- **The dev/prod two-account runbook** — project-specific and genuine, but a *single* rule in territory adjacent to the existing `local/tldr` pack; adding to an existing local pack is growth-extract's job, and a lone rule doesn't mint a pack.

**This repo should declare the canon `aws-sam` pack** rather than growing a local one. A technology can look unhomed here purely because its canon pack was never declared — which is exactly the `aws-sam` trap.
